findings.title: np.load allows pickle deserialization (arbitrary code execution)
findings.description: read_frame() calls np.load(path) without allow_pickle=False. NumPy defaults to allow_pickle=True, which means any .npz file can execute arbitrary Python code during deserialization via pickle payloads. Although cache files are written by the addon itself, an attacker who places a crafted .npz in the cache directory (e.g., via a compromised blend file or shared network path) can achieve remote code execution when the frame is loaded.
findings.impact: Arbitrary Python code execution when loading a malicious .npz cache file. In Blender this gives full access to the host system.
findings.fix: Add allow_pickle=False to the np.load() call: with np.load(path, allow_pickle=False) as data:

findings.title: No format version marker in any serialized file
findings.description: Cache .npz files, benchmark baselines, diagnostic reports, and exported OBJ/PLY files all lack a format version identifier. If the data schema changes (e.g., adding a new array to the npz, modifying benchmark field names, changing report structure), old serialized data will be silently misinterpreted, leading to data corruption, KeyErrors, or incorrect benchmark comparisons. There is no migration path because there is no way to detect the format version.
findings.impact: Forward-incompatible data corruption: future versions of the addon cannot distinguish old-format files from new, making safe schema migration impossible without manual deletion of all cached data.
findings.fix: Embed a version marker in every serialized artifact: (a) cache npz: add a 'format_version' array with a semver string; (b) benchmark/report JSON: add a top-level 'formatVersion' integer field; (c) validate the version on read and provide migration logic for older versions.

findings.title: No atomic writes anywhere in the codebase
findings.description: Every write path writes directly to the final destination file: cache.py: np.savez_compressed(path), export.py: open(path, 'w'), report.py: json.dump(report, fh), benchmark.py: json.dump(result, fh). A crash, power loss, or disk-full condition during any of these writes leaves a partial or corrupt file on disk. For cache frames this means a silently truncated .npz that cannot be read later. For benchmark baselines and reports it means data loss.
findings.impact: Partial or corrupt files on crash during write. Cache corruption leads to lost simulation frames; benchmark/report corruption loses diagnostic data.
findings.fix: Always write to a temporary file in the same directory, then os.replace(tmp_path, final_path) to atomically replace on POSIX/Windows. E.g.: import tempfile; fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=os.path.dirname(path)); os.write(fd, ...); os.close(fd); os.replace(tmp, path).

findings.title: JSON serialization can emit non-standard NaN/Inf values
findings.description: Profiler.to_json() calls json.dumps() with default allow_nan=True, which silently converts float('inf') and float('nan') to JavaScript NaN/Infinity tokens that are not valid JSON. Similarly report.py:write_report() uses json.dump() with allow_nan=True. Timer data from GPU profiling or compute_profile() derived memory tallies could produce non-finite values. Downstream JSON parsers that follow RFC 8259 strictly will reject the output.
findings.impact: Generated JSON reports may be unparseable by standards-compliant tools, breaking CI pipelines, external analysis scripts, or web-based report viewers.
findings.fix: Sanitize data before serialization: replace NaN with null and Inf with a large sentinel value (e.g., 1e30), or pass allow_nan=False and catch/handle ValueError. For timer dicts: {k: (v if math.isfinite(v) else 0.0) for k, v in data.items()}.

findings.title: Missing directory creation before export writes
findings.description: export_surface_obj() and export_points_ply() call open(path, 'w') without ensuring the parent directory exists. If the user specifies a non-existent directory, the write fails with FileNotFoundError. The cache.py write_frame() correctly calls os.makedirs(base, exist_ok=True), but export.py, report.py write_report(), and benchmark.py save_benchmark() do not.
findings.impact: Export, report generation, or benchmark save fails with an unhandled FileNotFoundError if the target directory does not already exist.
findings.fix: Add os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True) before opening the file in each write function.

findings.title: No error handling for corrupt .npz reads
findings.description: read_frame() delegates directly to np.load(path) with no try/except guard. If the .npz file is corrupt (partial write from a previous crash, manual modification, disk error), np.load raises a ValueError or OSError that propagates unhandled. No call site in the current codebase invokes read_frame(), but it is a public API function that downstream code could call.
findings.impact: Corrupt cache files cause unhandled exceptions that crash the read operation with no fallback or user-visible error message.
findings.fix: Wrap np.load in a try/except that returns None on failure (consistent with the existing None return for missing files), and optionally log the error.

findings.title: SolverSettings dataclass has no serialization or versioning support
findings.description: SolverSettings is a plain @dataclass with no to_dict(), from_dict(), or serialization round-trip methods. There is no format version field embedded in the dataclass. If new fields are added in a future version, old serialized settings will silently adopt default values, potentially changing simulation behavior. The Blender bridge (build_settings) copies fields manually over 50+ lines, which is brittle and misses any new fields.
findings.impact: Settings version skew: adding/removing fields in SolverSettings silently changes behavior when loading old data, with no migration path.
findings.fix: Add a 'settings_version' field to SolverSettings. Implement to_dict() that includes version, and from_dict(cls, data) classmethod with version-based migration. Replace the manual copy in build_settings() with a versioned serialization round-trip.

findings.title: FluidSolver GPU state has no save/restore mechanism
findings.description: FluidSolver holds all simulation state on the GPU (wp.array): particle positions/velocities, grid fields, velocity fields, whitewater state, churn field, etc. There is no to_dict() or serialization method to persist this state to disk and reload it later. The only persistable artifacts are cached frame snapshots (positions/velocities via cache.py) and surface meshes (via export.py). A full solver state capture would require downloading every GPU array and saving with metadata.
findings.impact: Simulation state is lost on Blender close or solver re-initialization. Users cannot save a simulation in progress and resume it later. Long-running simulations must complete in a single session.
findings.fix: Implement a save_state(path) method that downloads all GPU arrays to host numpy arrays via .numpy(), serializes settings, frame count, sim_time, and emit_seed, and writes to a .npz archive. Load_state(path) reverses the process. Include format version metadata.

findings.title: Enum property lookups fail on unknown values (forward-compatibility)
findings.description: build_settings() and build_snippets() resolve enum property strings with EnumType[fs.prop_value] (e.g., ParticleSampleType[fs.sample_type], CustomKernelArgumentMode[apg.mode]). If a .blend file was saved with a newer version of the addon that introduced new enum members, the lookup raises a KeyError and the entire settings build fails. There is no fallback, default, or migration for unknown enum values.
findings.impact: Loading a .blend file saved with a future version of the addon causes a hard crash during solver initialization, with no user-friendly recovery.
findings.fix: Wrap each enum lookup in a try/except KeyError with a fallback to a safe default. Log a warning for unrecognized values. Consider storing enum values as integers (stable across versions) rather than names.

findings.title: O(n) list pop(0) on profiler history trim
findings.description: Profiler.collect() appends each frame's timer dict to self.history and, when the list exceeds max_history (600), calls self.history.pop(0). pop(0) on a Python list is O(n) because every remaining element must be shifted. Over thousands of frames this produces quadratic complexity in the profiler's hot path (called every step_frame).
findings.impact: Degraded profiler performance during long simulations; the profiler overhead grows linearly with history length on each frame.
findings.fix: Use collections.deque(maxlen=max_history) instead of list + manual pop(0). deque.append() and automatic eviction are both O(1).

findings.title: JSON report write has no directory creation and no atomicity
findings.description: write_report() calls open(path, 'w', encoding='utf-8') then json.dump(report, fh). It does not create the parent directory (unlike cache.py's os.makedirs). It does not use atomic write. If the directory does not exist, the write fails. If the write is interrupted mid-dump, a partial JSON file is left on disk.
findings.impact: Report generation fails if the target directory is missing; partial JSON file remains on crash.
findings.fix: Add os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True) and use a temp-file + os.replace pattern for atomic writes.

findings.title: Benchmark baseline load has no schema validation
findings.description: load_benchmark() calls json.load(fh) and returns the resulting dict without validating that it contains the expected fields (BENCHMARK_FIELDS). If the baseline file is corrupt, modified by hand, or from a different version of the addon, compare_benchmark() will silently treat missing fields as None/0, producing misleading comparison results instead of failing clearly.
findings.impact: Silent mis-comparison against a corrupt or version-mismatched baseline, potentially reporting 'pass' when data is wrong or 'fail' for nonsensical reasons.
findings.fix: Add a validate_baseline(data) function that checks all expected BENCHMARK_FIELDS exist, verifies expected types, and checks a format_version field. Raise ValueError with a clear message on failure.

findings.title: _collider_prev velocity tracking state is lost across Blender sessions
findings.description: Session._collider_prev is a plain Python dict mapping object names to (translation, frame) tuples, used by _object_velocity() to estimate rigid-body velocity via frame differencing. This state is held only in memory on the Session singleton. If the Blender session is saved and reloaded (via .blend), or if the solver is re-initialized, the dict is cleared, causing collider velocities to be incorrectly reported as zero for the first frame after reload.
findings.impact: Animated colliders start with zero velocity for one frame after .blend reload or solver re-init, producing a small visual pop. For fast-moving colliders this may cause a brief fluid leak.
findings.fix: Store a persistent per-object velocity offset in the object's fluidSim property group, or serialize _collider_prev to a JSON/Blender custom property on save and restore on load.

findings.title: OBJ export does not validate mesh topology before writing
findings.description: export_surface_obj() writes OBJ faces as 'f {t[0]+1} {t[1]+1} {t[2]+1}' for every row in the tris array. If the input mesh contains degenerate triangles (zero-area), negative indices, or indices >= verts length, the OBJ file is silently malformed. Some DCC applications may fail to import such files or produce corrupted geometry.
findings.impact: Exported OBJ files with degenerate topology may fail to import in downstream tools, or produce corrupted meshes without warning.
findings.fix: Add a validation step before writing: filter out triangles where any index is negative or >= len(verts), or skip triangles with two or more equal indices. Log a warning with the count of skipped faces.

findings.title: No GPU data read-back validation for exports and cache writes
findings.description: particle_positions(), particle_velocities(), whitewater_positions(), and surface_mesh() all perform GPU-to-host readback via .numpy() but never validate the returned data. There are no NaN/Inf checks, no bounds checks, and no cardinality checks on the host side before the data is written to cache .npz files or exported OBJ/PLY files. If a GPU kernel produces corrupt output, the corruption is silently persisted.
findings.impact: Silent persistence of corrupt GPU data to disk. A transient GPU error produces a permanently corrupted cache or export file.
findings.fix: Add a lightweight host-side validation step on readback data: check for NaN/Inf in float arrays, verify indices are in-bounds for triangle meshes, and clamp or reject obviously invalid values before writing to disk.
